title: Music streaming
brief: People search for songs, build playlists and press play. The audio is the heavy part, and a hit song is played by millions at once. Playback must not stutter, even when part of your system fails.

clarify.q: Can the music keep playing if the playlist service is down?
clarify.a: It should. A song that has started must finish even when your database has a bad moment.
Spread across three continents. A listener far from your servers waits longer to start a song.

clarify.q: What happens on a big album release day?
clarify.a: Millions press play on the same few songs within minutes. This is your hottest data of the year.
Fast and forgiving. People mistype names. Results should arrive in well under half a second.

notes: An average song is about 5 MB (approx.); the game counts 2 MB stream chunks.
Playlist edits must show up for the person who made them straight away.

hints: What should still work if your main region goes dark for half an hour?
Songs never change, so a CDN with a long cache time can keep music playing even when your database is down. Search is a separate copy of your catalog: use a search index.
Playlist mutation retries must be idempotent; cached playlist views may lag within the declared contract. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Split the system into two halves. The audio path (CDN and object storage) holds songs that never change, so it can survive without the playlist database. The account path (playlists, library, play counts) needs a database and care about who sees what. A hit song is just one very hot cached key.

designs.name: Audio on the CDN, accounts behind it
designs.why: The CDN serves songs, so a regional outage or a hot album does not touch the origin. App servers in three zones handle search, playlists and play counts. A cache protects the database, and play events go through a queue so a busy minute never blocks playback.

tradeoffs: Keeping songs on the CDN with a long cache time makes playback survive almost any outage, but a song taken down for rights reasons needs an explicit purge.
A search index is a copy of the catalog. It is fast and forgiving, but it can be a few seconds behind the real catalog.
Reading playlists from a replica is cheaper, but it can show an old playlist right after an edit. The requirement asks you to show the editor their own change.
Play counts go through a queue so a flood of "song played" events cannot slow down audio. The counts arrive a little late, and nobody minds.
editorial.realWorld: Large music services play most songs from CDN and on-device caches (approx.). A new release from a top artist can make one track account for a noticeable share of all plays for a day.

correctness.prompt: Music streaming: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Keep playback independent of discovery and playlist failures. Playback and discovery have different failure boundaries. Origin protection matters during cold starts, not only at steady hit rates. Playlist mutation retries must be idempotent; cached playlist views may lag within the declared contract.

fields.label: Step 1. Search fails after playback has started. What should the player use?
options: Require a fresh search result for every chunk
The current manifest and buffered audio continue
fields.explanation: Playback and discovery have different failure boundaries.

fields.label: Step 2. An album becomes hot and its edge copy is cold. What protects storage?
options: Independent origin fetches from every viewer
Coalesced fills and bounded origin requests with buffered playback
fields.explanation: Origin protection matters during cold starts, not only at steady hit rates.

fields.label: Step 3. A playlist edit commits but the reply is lost. Retry how?
options: Append the song again because the response was missing
Use the edit id and version; return the committed edit once
fields.explanation: Playlist mutation retries must be idempotent; cached playlist views may lag within the declared contract.

correctness.responsibility: Keep playback independent of discovery and playlist failures.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 125 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $17481. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
